catalog_quote: The East Bodish languages Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala and Chali share a tonal system which exhibits less contrasts than the Central Bodish languages. I have no field notes for ’Nyenkha and Black Mountain, but given the fact that the other languages in the family report a nearly identical system, I suspect ’Nyenkha and Black Mountain would have a similar tonal system as well. Data from Kurtöp and Dakpa will be used to illustrate the East Bodish tone system, which is characterized as follows. Tone (high/low) is contrastive on the first syllable of words, following sonorant consonants. Unlike in Dzongkha, there does not appear to be salient glottalization concomitant with high tone. ... new_statements.quote: The East Bodish languages Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala and Chali share a tonal system which exhibits less contrasts than the Central Bodish languages. [...] Tone (high/low) is contrastive on the first syllable of words, following sonorant consonants. Unlike in Dzongkha, there does not appear to be salient glottalization concomitant with high tone. [...] Following obstruents, tone is not contrastive but instead predictable. As shown in Hyslop (2009), high tone follows voiceless initials and low tone follows voiced initials. [...] An identical system is found in Dakpa, Chali, Dzala, Bumthap and Khengkha.
new_statements.citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2010. Tone and tonogenesis in Bhutan: degrees of tonality? In Heather Bliss, Meagan Louie & Murray Schellenberg (eds.), Proceedings of NWLC 2009 (University of British Columbia Working Papers in Linguistics 25), 114-124. Vancouver: UBCWPL.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (+ text layer, 247 PDF pages, whole NWLC 2009 volume). Every sentence of the quoted passage is present verbatim in sec. 2.3 'East Bodish tonal system': 'The East Bodish languages Kurtöp, Bumthang, Khengkha, Dakpa, Dzala and Chali share a tonal system which exhibits less contrasts than the Central Bodish languages.'.. 'Tone (high/low) is contrastive on the first syllable of words, following sonorant consonants. Unlike in Dzongkha, there does not appear to be salient glottalization concomitant with high tone.'.. 'Following obstruents, tone is not contrastive but instead predictable. As shown in Hyslop (2009), high tone follows voiceless initials and low tone follows voiced initials.'..…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chali is described as a (marginally) tonal language of the East Bodish type: a high/low register tone contrast restricted to the first syllable of the word after sonorant initials, with tone fully predictable from initial voicing after obstruents. The source says nothing about word stress; no stress statement for Chali exists in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the Kurtöp palatal fricative exception is given; nothing Chali-specific. Chali itself is covered by the one sentence 'An identical system is found in Dakpa, Chali, Dzala, Bumthap and Khengkha' (illustrated with Kurtöp and Dakpa data, not Chali data).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('first syllable of words'); the description is by generalization across East Bodish from the author's field notes, not from a Chali data set.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyslop's 'Chali' = Glottolog chal1267 Chalikha [tgf] (Chalipkha, Chalipakha; village of Chali, Mongar District). No dialect distinctions are made in any source seen. Note that Bodt 2023 (the source named by the earlier scan) does not treat Chali data at all; it only places Chali in the East Bodish phylogeny.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'East Bodish tonal system' (pp. 116-117, PDF pp. 123-124): Chali shares the East Bodish system, high/low tone contrastive on the first syllable after sonorants, predictable after obstruents; 'An identical system is found in Dakpa, Chali, Dzala, Bumthap and Khengkha.' Author has field notes for these languages (says she lacks them only for 'Nyenkha and Black Mountain). Nothing at all on stress.
